strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and timely interdisciplinary problem: using neural evidence about predictive processing to improve fMRI-to-language reconstruction.

The proposed PREDFT architecture is reasonably coherent, combining a 3D-CNN/FIR/Transformer decoding network with a side network that predicts future words from selected cortical regions and fuses this information through cross-attention.

The empirical study is broader than a single end-to-end comparison: it includes predictive-coding verification, ROI selection, prediction-distance analysis, case studies, decoding-error analysis, side-network ablation, and sensitivity to the joint-loss weight.
Using cross-subject splitting and fMRIPrep preprocessing shows awareness of the data-leakage concerns that have affected prior brain-to-text work.
PREDFT shows substantial gains over the no-side-network setting and improvements over UniCoRN on several primary metrics, especially BLEU-1 for longer fMRI sequences.
weaknesses: The central neurocognitive claim is stronger than the evidence. An auxiliary future-word-prediction loss does not by itself establish that the model captures brain predictive coding; the effect could also reflect contextual language prediction, delayed BOLD responses, additional model capacity, or generic feature learning.

Critical controls are missing. The paper should compare against temporally shuffled future-word labels, a non-predictive auxiliary task, text-only future prediction, and capacity-matched side networks that do not use the selected ROIs. The fact that whole-cortex input also performs well weakens the claim that the six BPC regions are uniquely responsible.

The temporal setup needs much greater clarity. The FIR component already incorporates future fMRI frames, and the cross-attention mask allows later side-network representations to attend to earlier text tokens. The paper must demonstrate that this is offline use of observed brain signals rather than target leakage or future-state decoding, and distinguish it from genuine current-state prediction.

The state-of-the-art claim is not fully supported because only one comparable baseline, UniCoRN, is evaluated. Other recent systems are excluded because of preprocessing or splitting differences, but no reimplementation or alternative-protocol comparison is provided.

There are no confidence intervals, significance tests, or results across multiple random seeds. Some metric differences are small, and UniCoRN outperforms PREDFT on several BLEU-4 or ROUGE-precision entries, so the claimed overall superiority depends on selecting particular metrics.

BLEU and ROUGE alone are inadequate for evaluating generated language. The case studies show considerable disfluency and semantic error; at minimum, semantic-similarity metrics and/or human evaluation should be included.

The predictive-coding verification uses ROIs already motivated by prior literature rather than an exploratory whole-brain analysis, and multiple-comparison correction is not reported. It is also unclear whether the added future-word features are evaluated in a fully held-out setting that prevents improved fit from merely adding predictors.

Reproducibility is only partially adequate. The appendix provides useful settings, but the paper does not state whether code/models will be released, and it lacks exact train/test subject and story counts, story-overlap controls, random seeds, some architectural dimensions, and a precise description of how future-word targets are constructed and used at inference.

The proposed information-loss slope and positional error analysis are exploratory and ad hoc, with no statistical validation. The ablation study also does not isolate components such as the FIR module, attention mask, shared embeddings, or side-network decoder.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and relevant problem at the intersection of NLP and cognitive neuroscience: reconstructing language from fMRI signals.
The proposed PredFT model is conceptually coherent, combining a standard fMRI-to-text decoding network with an auxiliary side network and cross-attention fusion.

The preliminary predictive-coding analysis, ROI selection, prediction-distance study, error analysis, ablations, and hyper-parameter analysis provide several complementary ways to examine the proposed mechanism.
PredFT outperforms a re-run UniCoRN baseline on several metrics, especially BLEU-1 and ROUGE-1 F, under the authors' preprocessing and splitting protocol.
The appendix supplies useful implementation details, including the atlas, model dimensions, optimization schedule, hardware, and preprocessing choices.
weaknesses: The state-of-the-art claim is not adequately supported. Only UniCoRN is directly compared, while Tang et al. and BrainLLM are excluded because of setting differences; fair reimplementations or comparisons on identical splits are needed.

The evidence for predictive coding is correlational and does not rule out simpler explanations. The FIR module uses future fMRI frames, which may contain BOLD responses to the so-called future words, creating a potential temporal-information leakage issue.

The paper needs stricter leakage controls, such as models without future TRs, lag-matched non-predictive controls, shuffled future targets, and clarification that training stories and subjects are disjoint.

Evaluation relies almost entirely on BLEU and ROUGE. These overlap metrics, especially BLEU-1, can reward common words and do not adequately measure semantic correctness or fluency; human evaluation and embedding-based semantic metrics are necessary.

No statistical significance tests, confidence intervals across seeds or subjects, or variance estimates are provided. Several metric differences are small or inconsistent, and PredFT is not better on every metric.

The qualitative outputs remain highly disfluent and only partially capture the reference, which weakens the claim of coherent language reconstruction despite the relatively favorable automatic scores.

Reproducibility is incomplete: no code release is stated, and the exact train/validation/test split, split sizes, value of k*, inference behavior of the side network, ridge-regression details, and model-selection protocol for lambda are unclear.
Generalizability is limited because all experiments use only the Narratives dataset and one cross-subject setting; external datasets and per-subject comparisons are absent.

Some neurological and causal claims are stronger than the model-based evidence supports, and the notation, attention-mask description, and temporal indexing contain ambiguities that make the method harder to verify.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and relevant intersection of computational linguistics, NLP, and cognitive neuroscience: reconstructing natural language from fMRI while exploiting predictive-coding structure.

The proposed PREDFT model is coherent and reasonably complete, combining a 3D-CNN/FIR encoder, Transformer-based main decoder, ROI-based predictive side network, cross-attention fusion, and a joint training objective.
The preliminary predictive-coding analysis and the subsequent ROI-based model design are well connected, making the architecture more interpretable than a purely black-box fMRI-to-text system.

Experiments on the large Narratives dataset use cross-subject splitting and multiple fMRI context lengths; PREDFT outperforms the directly comparable UniCoRN baseline on most reported metrics, reaching a BLEU-1 score of 27.80%.

The paper includes useful supporting analyses of ROI selection, prediction distance, decoding-error position, side-network ablation, and the joint-loss weight \lambda, giving several diagnostic views of where the proposed gains arise.

The methodology and appendices provide substantial implementation detail, including atlas choice, model depths, preprocessing, optimization schedule, context lengths, and hardware, which supports reproducibility.
weaknesses: The empirical comparison is narrower than the state-of-the-art claims imply. Only UniCoRN is directly compared; Tang et al. and BrainLLM are excluded because of preprocessing or split incompatibility. Re-running or reimplementing these methods under the same setting would substantially strengthen the paper.

Results are not accompanied by variance across random seeds, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests. Several metric differences are small, and UniCoRN occasionally wins individual metrics, so 'state-of-the-art' and 'best overall performance' should be qualified.

The evidence does not fully establish a specifically predictive-coding explanation. Future-word predictability can be entangled with BOLD hemodynamic delay, temporal smoothing, and the FIR representation. Additional controls such as shuffled future words, lag-matched controls, or non-predictive auxiliary tasks would make the causal interpretation more convincing.

The side-network benefit is somewhat inconsistent across metrics. In Table 2, whole-cortex or random-ROI variants perform comparably or better on several measures, and the advantage of the six BPC ROIs is not uniformly dominant without paired statistical testing.

Evaluation relies on BLEU and ROUGE, while the generated texts remain quite disfluent. Semantic metrics such as BERTScore or embedding-based similarity, together with a small human evaluation, would better assess whether recovered content is semantically faithful rather than lexically overlapping.

Reproducibility would be improved by releasing the exact subject-level splits, preprocessing filters, decoding algorithm and hyperparameters, random seeds, model size/parameter count, trained checkpoints, and code. It should also be stated explicitly how the side network operates at inference without access to ground-truth future words.

All experiments use one dataset and cross-subject evaluation only. Generalization to other naturalistic fMRI datasets and to within-subject settings remains untested, although the authors acknowledge this as a limitation.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and relevant interdisciplinary problem at the intersection of NLP, naturalistic language understanding, and neural decoding.

The proposed PredFT architecture is clearly motivated and combines a main fMRI-to-text decoding network with a side network trained on future-word targets, joint losses, and a dedicated predictive-coding attention mechanism.

The empirical study is broad: it uses two naturalistic fMRI datasets, within-subject and cross-subject settings, several sequence lengths, multiple strong baselines, BLEU/ROUGE/BERTScore, ROI variants, hyperparameter analysis, shuffled-input controls, error analysis, and case studies.

The full model consistently improves over the no-side-network variant and performs better than or comparably to recent baselines on many metrics, supporting the practical utility of the side signal as an auxiliary representation.
The manuscript includes substantial implementation detail in the appendices, including preprocessing, model dimensions, training schedules, notation, and supplementary analyses.
weaknesses: The central predictive-coding interpretation is temporally confounded. The FIR module and predictive-coding mask allow a decoder at time t to use later fMRI representations. Because BOLD is a delayed and smoothed post-stimulus signal, those later frames may contain hemodynamic responses to the supposedly predicted words rather than evidence of pre-stimulus brain prediction. A strict temporal availability cutoff, causal attention, and HRF-aware controls are needed, or the contribution should be reframed as offline future-context fusion.

The prediction score P(d,l) is not sufficient causal evidence. Future embeddings are obtained from the known transcript, and improvements may arise from HRF overlap, speech coarticulation, narrative context, linguistic predictability, or temporal autocorrelation. Missing controls include past-word targets, shuffled or impossible future targets, and context-only baselines.

The decoding results lack statistical uncertainty: there are no multiple-seed results, standard deviations, bootstrap confidence intervals, or significance tests for metric differences. With only one reported split and three LeBel subjects, claims of outperforming prior models are not fully secure.

Reproducibility could be strengthened. The exact LeBel train/validation/test split, treatment of overlapping windows, final prediction length and distance used for LeBel, definition of k*, random seeds, and code/model release are not clearly specified in the main manuscript.

The ROI definitions are inconsistent. The main text describes BPC ROIs such as STS, IFG, SMG, and angular gyrus, while the appendix states that an “Auditory” parcel is used for LeBel. If the latter is true, gains may reflect richer sensory cortex input rather than predictive regions.

Despite metric improvements, the generated examples remain highly repetitive and often ungrammatical, with very low BLEU-4 scores. Without human evaluation or stronger semantic evaluation, claims about coherent or fluent language reconstruction should be tempered.

strengths: Addresses a relevant and timely problem at the intersection of NLP, cognitive neuroscience, and fMRI-to-text decoding.

PREDFT introduces a plausible auxiliary side-network design: a side encoder is trained with future-word prediction and fused into the main decoder, while the side decoder is discarded at inference, so future transcripts are not directly required during testing.

The empirical scope is reasonably broad, covering two naturalistic fMRI datasets, within-subject and cross-subject settings, recent baselines, multiple automatic metrics, ROI comparisons, prediction-horizon analysis, shuffled-input chance controls, ablations, and error analysis.
The full model generally improves over the no-side-network variant, especially on BLEU-1 and ROUGE1-F, and the analysis of late-position decoding errors is an interesting diagnostic.
The appendix provides substantial architectural and hyperparameter detail, including a FIR component intended to compensate for BOLD latency.
weaknesses: The central predictive-coding verification is not cleanly identified. The gain from adding future-word features may arise from within-TR co-occurrence, BOLD/timing misalignment, contextual semantic overlap, or increased input dimensionality. A lag-aware receptive-window control, acoustic/phonetic covariates, future-versus-past comparison, and permuted-future null distribution are missing.

The ablations do not isolate future prediction as the causal mechanism. Removing the side network simultaneously removes ROI input, an auxiliary loss, cross-attention, and model capacity. A matched side network predicting current or past words, or shuffled targets, is needed. The no-side-network model also already beats several baselines, indicating that much of the gain may come from the base architecture.

Statistical robustness is limited. There are no multi-seed results, bootstrap confidence intervals, or significance tests, and the within-subject analysis relies on only three participants. Some metrics, including ROUGE recall and BLEU-4 in several settings, still favor baselines, so the broad outperformance claims should be qualified.

Automatic metrics do not establish coherent language reconstruction. The displayed outputs remain highly disfluent, repetitive, and hallucinated, and there is no human or semantic-faithfulness evaluation to complement BLEU, ROUGE, and BERTScore.

Reproducibility and notation are only partly adequate. Code, checkpoints, and exact split identifiers are not provided; the FIR dimensions are ambiguous; the construction of the future-word sequence and its relationship to prediction length and distance are unclear; and the BPC ROI definitions differ across datasets and appendix descriptions.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and relevant intersection of computational neuroscience and NLP: explicitly operationalizing brain predictive coding as an auxiliary signal for fMRI-to-language reconstruction.

The proposed PredFT architecture is conceptually clear: a main encoder-decoder performs decoding, while a side network learns ROI-based future-word prediction, and predictive-coding attention fuses this information during training before the side decoder is discarded at inference.

The preliminary predictive-coding verification is useful and motivates the model design, especially the dependence of prediction scores on prediction length, prediction distance, and selected brain regions.

The empirical evaluation is broad, covering within-subject decoding on LeBel and cross-subject decoding on Narratives, multiple fMRI sequence lengths, several strong recent baselines, and multiple automatic metrics.

The paper includes informative analyses beyond headline results: ROI selection, prediction-length/distance grids, hyperparameter sensitivity, shuffled-input chance controls, error-position analysis, ablations, and qualitative examples.

Across the primary decoding metrics, particularly BLEU-1 and ROUGE-1 F, PredFT shows consistent improvements over the no-side-network variant and competitive or better performance relative to existing methods.
The manuscript is generally well organized, with detailed architecture figures, a notation table, and substantial implementation detail in the appendices.
weaknesses: Statistical evidence is limited: there are no reported random seeds, run-to-run variances, confidence intervals, paired bootstrap tests, or significance tests for decoding improvements. The LeBel analysis also relies on only three subjects.

The gains are modest and metric-dependent. PredFT does not uniformly improve BERTScore, ROUGE recall, or BLEU-4, and the absolute generation quality remains low; qualitative outputs still contain substantial grammatical and lexical errors.

The predictive-coding verification may be affected by temporal autocorrelation, BOLD hemodynamic smoothing, and correlated language-model features. Permutation controls or matched non-predictive future representations are needed to show that the small positive scores genuinely reflect prediction rather than temporal alignment.

The BPC ROIs are identified using analyses on the same datasets on which decoding is subsequently evaluated, raising a possible selection-bias concern. Independent held-out datasets or modalities would strengthen the spatial claims.

Because PredFT without the side network also performs strongly, part of the advantage may come from the overall encoder-decoder architecture rather than predictive coding specifically. The experiments demonstrate empirical benefit but do not conclusively establish the proposed cognitive mechanism.

Evaluation relies entirely on automatic metrics. Human semantic evaluation would be valuable for open-ended fMRI reconstruction, where BLEU and ROUGE have known limitations and BERTScore may not fully capture coherence.

Reproducibility would be improved by an explicit code release, exact train/validation/test story-level split descriptions, random seeds, and clearer reporting of how future-word targets and ROI sequences are aligned for each subject.

Some notation and alignment details are difficult to follow, including the dimensions used in the brain-score correlation, the precise construction of future representations, and the interaction between the predictive-coding mask and teacher-forced decoder inputs.
